rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and the capital hosts one of the region's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. The capital's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

The consequence axis of an arrest is largely undocumented: no source in this record describes how transgender prisoners are housed in the country's civilian prison system — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice — and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced. The one documented trans placement case inside the country's custody system is military rather than civilian: a transgender conscript was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; a district court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the defence ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty — a harsh institutional default corrected by the courts only after death. For a detained trans visitor, civilian prison placement is simply unknown: in a legal system where legal gender recognition is possible and courts have repeatedly ruled for trans people, recourse would likely exist, but the placement practice itself is unverified — not a verified midpoint and not verified safe.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Compared with its closest comparable peers, the legal baseline has documented gaps: no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage. Policy and litigation flux: a December 2024 martial-law crisis and related assembly-freedom questions, a 2024 constitutional ruling recognising same-sex partners' healthcare rights, and organised conservative opposition set a moving political backdrop rather than direct street-level risk.

Custody-axis framing: the only trans placement case inside the country's custody system on record is a military conscript case — a conscript's discharge, death, posthumous reinstatement and line-of-duty recognition — rather than a civilian prison case; the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel (the military criminal code, article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment) and the exclusion of transgender people from military service are resident-conscript-facing, not visitor-facing.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The court-based legal gender recognition process (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it), the hospital-ward 'transgender blind spot' (the health ministry cannot answer how to accommodate trans patients), school-bathroom friction, and the military-service harassment data (12% of trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military experienced sexual harassment or violence — this affects conscripts, not foreign visitors) are all resident-facing.

Further resident data: 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers; same-sex conduct is criminalised in the military under the military criminal code (upheld in 2023); and a nationwide survey documents a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

The one documented institutional case is a conscript's: the individual stood under mandatory military service and the military criminal code — legal machinery that does not reach visitors; transgender people are excluded from military service, and the military same-sex-conduct ban governs serving personnel, while nothing is documented about how trans people are housed in the civilian prison system at all.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Foreign-tourist taxi scams and shopping complaints rose 71% in 2024 — general, not trans-specific.

One source — a supreme-court family-register decision — could not be retrieved at research time, so that ruling's detail rests on its summary. No border-screening or document-handling practice specific to trans visitors is documented in this record.

Prison axis: no rule, regulation, case or practice is documented on civilian trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, no solitary/segregation practice; the only placement case on record is the military discharge case (an administrative discharge, not a prison-housing case). Where a detained trans visitor would be housed in the civilian system is unverified, and that gap cannot be read as evidence of either identity-based placement or mistreatment.
blindSourceSummaries: A July 2024 court judgment, final with no appeal: police advising a trans person undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, with symbolic compensation awarded for the infringement.

A May 2024 court ruling: a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery to change legal sex status — five plaintiffs assigned male at birth and on hormone therapy for years; the court held that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals.
A March 2024 research report: trans teens avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; researchers urged law and institutional reforms for safer school environments.

A November 2023 report: the national human-rights watchdog flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalisation' — the health ministry rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

A country overview (updated March 2026): civilian same-sex conduct legal but criminalised in the military under the military criminal code, upheld in 2023; legal gender recognition possible; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey (June 2025): hundreds of transgender and non-binary young adults mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages, documenting a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

A 2025 annual report chapter: a relatively positive record with free media and civil society but persistent documented discrimination, also covering a December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms.

A travel guide (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to the capital's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods but requiring contextual understanding — military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a 2024 constitutional ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

A source not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying entry covers a supreme-court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

An encyclopedic overview: no dedicated coverage of trans prisoners; documents the only prominent trans placement case, military rather than civilian — a conscript discharged in early 2020, death by suicide in March 2021, posthumous reinstatement by a district court on 7 October 2021, and line-of-duty recognition in March 2024; consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised (article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment); transgender people are excluded from military service; no information on civilian trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states/provinces offer administrative legal gender recognition; the capital and one other state/province have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist. Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the region — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and the heavily policed, progressively governed capital, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is the country's general crime environment; state/province-level scores range from among the region's best to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is undocumented: the only prison-axis finding in this record — a survey of LGBTQ people in prison — contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement in the country (no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice); its sole country-specific item is a July 2007 policy in the capital, adopted through the human-rights commission, allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. In a nation where legal gender recognition is decided separately in each state/province and official discrimination and near-total impunity for anti-trans violence are documented, where a detained trans visitor would be housed is unverifiable and cannot be assumed to follow identity.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Marriage equality nationwide — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Custody-policy context: the sole country-specific prison finding in this record — the capital's July 2007 same-sex conjugal-visit policy stemming from a 2003 anti-discrimination law, applying to all the capital's prisons, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate — is a local custody-conditions measure, not a placement rule; it shows local recognition of sexual-orientation rights inside one city's prisons without any documented counterpart for trans-prisoner placement anywhere in the country.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The administrative legal gender recognition regime, which varies by state/province, and the transfemicide statutes (in the capital and one other state/province) are resident-facing; the 71-murder toll falls overwhelmingly on local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit.

Resident custody: the documented prison-axis finding — the 2007 same-sex conjugal-visit policy in the capital, applying to all its prisons — governs inmates; the undocumented trans-prisoner placement practice (no birth-sex vs identity rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation data in any source in this record) concerns residents held in the system; a visitor meets either only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Cartel violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several governments to advise caution or non-essential travel avoidance for parts of the country — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.

Prison axis: the single prison-axis source is thin for this country — it documents no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units and no solitary/segregation practice, and its only country-specific item (the 2007 policy in the capital on same-sex conjugal visits) says nothing about where trans prisoners are housed; whether a detained trans visitor would be held by the national authorities or by a state/province, and how documents would interact with placement, are unverified in these sources.
blindSourceSummaries: A March 2025 human-rights dispatch: calls on the country's state/province authorities to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many now have such procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist.

A March 2024 human-rights report: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in a river in August 2023.

A July 2024 news report: the capital's legislature approved a law criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

A January 2024 news report: a wave of transgender killings spurs protests — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including an activist shot in the capital, drawing outrage and street protests.

A 2024 regional body press release: urges national and state/province authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

A 2024 analysis: progressive legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors caution that earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people are safe from violence including murder.

A foreign government travel-advice page: exercise a high degree of caution nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional avoid-non-essential-travel advisories in some coastal areas.

A 2024 report: the capital's legislature approved the transfemicide law; regional monitoring records hundreds of transfemicides from 2008 to 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023 — second only to one other country's figure.

An encyclopedic survey of LGBTQ people in prison, country section: records only one country-specific policy — a July 2007 policy in the capital, adopted through the human-rights commission, allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation — and no data on trans-prisoner housing placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice.
